attribution: Original project-authored beginner grammar lessons and exercises.

lessons.title: A friendly introduction with です
lessons.summary: Use です (desu) to say what something is, politely.
lessons.concept: [Topic] は [description] です。 です makes a sentence polite.

steps.title: Meet です
steps.body: です (desu) turns a simple description into a polite sentence. わたしは学生です means ‘I am a student.’

steps.prompt: Which sentence means ‘I am a teacher’?
steps.feedback: Put the person first, then their description, and finish with です.

steps.prompt: Build: ‘I am a student.’
Trace the kana あ before you go.
Pair each Japanese particle with its job.
steps.feedback: Particles are small, but they do a big job!

lessons.title: Set the topic with は
lessons.summary: は (wa) marks what your sentence is about.
lessons.concept: [Topic] は [information] です。 The particle は is written ha, pronounced wa.

steps.title: The topic marker は
steps.body: は marks the topic: the thing you’re talking about. In this job, は is pronounced wa.

steps.prompt: Choose the topic marker for ‘As for me, I’m a student.’
steps.feedback: You found the topic! は tells us who or what the sentence is about.

steps.prompt: Complete: わたし ___ 学生です。 (I am a student.)
steps.hint: It is written ha, but said wa.

steps.prompt: Pair each Japanese particle with its job.
steps.feedback: Particles are small, but they do a big job!

lessons.title: Spotlight with が
lessons.summary: が (ga) marks a subject, often with likes and abilities.
lessons.concept: [Thing/person] が [liking or existence]. が can spotlight new information.

steps.title: A little spotlight: が
steps.body: が marks the subject that does, exists, or is liked. It often answers ‘what?’ or ‘who?’

steps.prompt: Which particle belongs in ‘I like music’? わたしは音楽 ___ 好きです。
steps.feedback: 好きです commonly pairs with が for the thing someone likes.

steps.prompt: Build: ‘There is a dog.’
Pair each Japanese particle with its job.
steps.feedback: Particles are small, but they do a big job!

lessons.title: Give actions an object with を
lessons.summary: を (o) marks what an action is done to.
lessons.concept: [Person] は [thing] を [verb]. を is pronounced o.

steps.title: The action’s target を
steps.body: を marks the direct object: the thing you read, eat, see, or buy. It is written wo and pronounced o.

steps.prompt: Listen and pick the particle you hear.
steps.feedback: 飲みます (drink) acts on water, so を marks it.

steps.prompt: Complete: パン ___ 食べます。 (I eat bread.)
Pair each Japanese particle with its job.
steps.feedback: Particles are small, but they do a big job!

lessons.title: Find a time or destination with に
lessons.summary: に (ni) can mark when something happens or where you’re going.
lessons.concept: [Time/place] に [action]. に points to a time or destination.

steps.title: A point in time or place
steps.body: に points to a destination or a specific time. Think of it as a little pin on the map or clock.

steps.prompt: Choose the particle for ‘I go to school.’ 学校 ___ 行きます。
steps.feedback: に marks the destination of 行きます (go). へ can also mark direction.

steps.prompt: Build: ‘I meet a friend at three.’
steps.answer: 三時に友だちに会います。
steps.translation: I meet a friend at three.

steps.prompt: Pair each Japanese particle with its job.
steps.feedback: Particles are small, but they do a big job!

lessons.title: Show where it happens with で
lessons.summary: で (de) marks where an action takes place or what tool you use.
lessons.concept: [Place/tool] で [action]. に often marks a destination; で marks the action’s setting.

steps.title: The action setting で
steps.body: Use で for the place where an action happens. Use に for a destination or for where something exists.
steps.japanese: 図書館で本を読みます。
steps.meaning: I read a book at the library.

steps.prompt: I eat at home: うち ___ 食べます。
steps.feedback: Eating is an action happening at home, so で fits.

steps.prompt: Build: ‘I study Japanese at school.’
steps.answer: 学校で日本語を勉強します。

steps.prompt: Pair each Japanese particle with its job.
steps.feedback: Particles are small, but they do a big job!

lessons.title: Polite everyday verbs: ます
lessons.summary: The ます form makes everyday actions polite.
lessons.concept: Verb stem + ます: 食べます (eat), 見ます (see), 行きます (go).

steps.title: A polite action ending
steps.body: ます is a friendly, polite ending for verbs. Japanese sentence endings carry the politeness, so the verb often comes last.
steps.japanese: 毎日日本語を勉強します。

steps.prompt: Which is the polite form of 読む (to read)?
steps.feedback: 読む changes to 読み, then add ます.

steps.prompt: Build: ‘I drink water.’
steps.answer: わたしは水を飲みます。

steps.prompt: Pair each Japanese particle with its job.
steps.feedback: Particles are small, but they do a big job!

lessons.title: Describe things with adjectives
lessons.summary: い-adjectives and な-adjectives have different sentence patterns.
lessons.concept: い-adjective + です. な-adjective + です (or な before a noun).

steps.title: Two adjective families
steps.body: い-adjectives like おいしい can go straight before です. な-adjectives like しずか use な before a noun: しずかな町.

steps.prompt: Complete: この本は ___ です。 (This book is interesting.)
steps.feedback: い-adjectives keep their い before です.

steps.prompt: Build: ‘It is a quiet town.’
Pair each Japanese particle with its job.
steps.feedback: Particles are small, but they do a big job!

lessons.title: Ask a gentle question with か
lessons.summary: Add か to the end of a polite sentence to make a question.
lessons.concept: Polite statement + か。 A question word stays where its answer belongs.

steps.title: A question with か
steps.body: Put か at the end of a polite sentence to turn it into a question. In writing, finish with 。 or ?.

steps.prompt: Where does か go in a polite question?
steps.feedback: Yes! か gives the whole sentence a question shape.

steps.prompt: Add the question particle: これは本です ___
Pair each Japanese particle with its job.
steps.feedback: Particles are small, but they do a big job!

lessons.title: Say ‘not’ politely
lessons.summary: Use じゃありません to politely say what something is not.
lessons.concept: Noun/adjective + じゃありません。 For verbs, ません replaces ます.

steps.title: A soft, polite ‘not’
steps.body: じゃありません makes a noun or な-adjective negative. Polite verbs use ません: 食べません (do not eat).

steps.prompt: How do you politely say ‘I do not drink’?
steps.feedback: For a polite verb negative, replace ます with ません.

steps.prompt: Build: ‘I am not a teacher.’
steps.answer: わたしは先生じゃありません。

steps.prompt: Pair each Japanese particle with its job.
steps.feedback: Particles are small, but they do a big job!
